answers.answer: SCOPe 2.08 puts all three in one superfamily: b.6.1 "Cupredoxins" (SUNID 49503), under fold b.6 "Cupredoxin-like" (SUNID 49502) and class b "All beta proteins". They are in three separate families of that superfamily: plastocyanin/azurin-like is b.6.1.1 (SUNID 49504), ephrin ectodomain is b.6.1.5 (SUNID 74874), and PAD4 N-terminal domain is b.6.1.6 (SUNID 110107). Within the superfamily, that is SCOPe's claim of probable distant common ancestry, backed by structure and not by close sequence similarity. At family level they are not the same family, which means they do not have clear, close homology. So the apparent biological unrelatedness is real at the level of function and sequence. The shared cupredoxin β-sandwich fold is the only link. Two SCOPe annotations make this explicit. The ephrin family comment reads "eukaryotic signaling domain probably related to cupredoxins but lacking the metal-binding site". The PAD4 N-terminal family comment reads "probably related to cupredoxins but lacking the metal-binding site". The superfamily itself is annotated "contains copper-binding site", but that describes the copper-binding members such as plastocyanin and azurin. It is not a property of every family in the superfamily. Copper binding and electron transfer should not be inferred across these families. Homology in SCOPe does not mean shared function or conserved active-site residues. The ephrin ectodomain is a receptor-binding signaling domain (Eph receptor ligand). The PAD4 N-terminal domain is a regulatory or structural domain of a peptidylarginine deiminase, and the catalytic domain is a separate domain at d.126.1.5. SCOPe says both lack the metal-binding site, so there is no basis to predict a copper site or redox activity in either. A copper site or electron-transfer role needs direct evidence, for example conserved ligand residues (the His/Cys/His/Met-type set), metal analysis, or spectroscopy. Even within the plastocyanin/azurin-like family, function transfer is limited to proteins that keep the ligands. Likewise, a template from one family should not be used for ligand, site or function modelling in another without that evidence. I did not check sequence alignments of conserved copper ligands myself. The conclusion rests on SCOPe's classification and its comments only.

SCOPe says both lack the metal-binding site, so there is no basis to predict a copper site or redox activity in either. A copper site or electron-transfer role needs direct evidence, for example conserved ligand residues (the His/Cys/His/Met-type set), metal analysis, or spectroscopy. Even within the plastocyanin/azurin-like family, function transfer is limited to proteins that keep the ligands. Likewise, a template from one family should not be used for ligand, site or function modelling in another without that evidence. I did not check sequence alignments of conserved copper ligands myself. The conclusion rests on SCOPe's classification and its comments only.
